EV Charger Connector Standards Explained: Type 2, CCS, and CHAdeMO in the UK Market

Buying an electric vehicle in the UK means navigating a bewildering array of charging options, and not all plugs are interchangeable. The connector on your EV dictates where you can charge, how quickly, and whether you'll find a suitable socket at public charging networks across the country. We've spent years helping UK drivers sort through the confusion. This guide covers the three main EV charger connector standards, Type 2, CCS, and CHAdeMO, and shows you exactly what each one means for home charging, long motorway trips, and deciding whether to buy a particular used electric vehicle.

What Are EV Charger Connector Standards and Why They Matter in the UK

An EV connector standard sets out the physical plug shape, pin layout, how the vehicle and charger communicate, and the maximum power they can handle. Without standards, every manufacturer would design its own socket, creating a fragmented mess where drivers couldn't charge across different networks. Standards prevent that chaos by giving everyone a common baseline.

The UK typically aligned itself with Europe's IEC 62196 framework, which covers both the Type 2 AC connector and its DC counterpart, the Combined Charging System (CCS). When the UK left the EU, it kept these standards to maintain compatibility with European charging infrastructure, a sensible decision given that vehicles and charging networks cross borders regularly.

This matters in real life. A connector mismatch means your car sits idle. Own an older Nissan LEAF with a CHAdeMO socket and pull into a service station with only CCS rapid chargers? You're stuck. Understanding these standards directly affects how far you can travel, what a used EV is worth, and the true cost of electric car ownership for hundreds of thousands of UK drivers.

Type 2 Connectors: The European Standard That Dominated UK Charging Infrastructure

The Type 2 connector, defined in IEC 62196-2, is a seven-pin AC plug and has become the widely adopted socket for slow and fast AC charging across the UK and Europe. It typically handles single-phase power at up to approximately 7.4 kW for home wallboxes and three-phase power at up to around 22 kW at public rapid AC chargers. Every mainstream EV sold in the UK since around 2015 has a Type 2 inlet, from the Volkswagen ID.4 to the Tesla Model 3.

The UK government's Electric Vehicle Homecharge Scheme and later grant programmes required home chargers to use Type 2, making it the default for residential installations. Out in public, lamp-post chargers, car park units, and hotel and supermarket destination chargers almost all use Type 2, making it the daily workhorse of UK EV charging.

Most UK drivers encounter Type 2 constantly, charging at home overnight or topping up during shopping trips. Its seven pins enable two-way conversation between car and charger, unlocking smart features such as scheduling charges for off-peak hours or balancing grid load. It doesn't match the speed of DC systems, but its sheer availability makes it essential. You can find EV charging points near you that support Type 2 AC charging across the UK in real time.

CCS (Combined Charging System) and CHAdeMO: Fast-Charging Standards Explained

When you need serious range in a hurry, at service stations or rapid charging hubs during long trips, DC fast charging takes over. Two competing DC standards have dominated the UK space: CCS and CHAdeMO. Knowing the difference matters for anyone shopping for or leasing an EV, because the two are completely incompatible without an adapter, and adapters are extremely difficult to find.

CCS, or CCS2 in Europe, adds two large DC pins below the Type 2 connector, creating a combined nine-pin interface. This means one socket on the vehicle typically handles both everyday AC charging and high-power DC rapid charging, with advanced systems theoretically reaching up to 350 kW, though most UK EVs currently accept between 50 kW and lower speeds. and 150 kW. Nearly every European, American, and Korean manufacturer has adopted CCS, including BMW, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Kia, Ford, and General Motors. It's now the dominant rapid charging standard in the UK.

CHAdeMO is a DC standard created by a Japanese industry group and originally pushed by Nissan and Mitsubishi. It uses a separate, larger round connector that sits alongside a Type 2 AC inlet on compatible cars. Most UK units typically max out at around 50 kW, though CHAdeMO 2.0 theoretically supports up to approximately 400 kW. In practice, UK charge point operators have steadily dropped CHAdeMO from new builds, pouring money into CCS instead. This has left owners of CHAdeMO vehicles increasingly short of rapid charging options.

Why Thousands of Older UK EVs Are Now Stranded With Obsolete Connectors

The UK's sharp shift to CCS has created real problems for owners of early-generation EVs. The original Nissan LEAF (2011–2017) used a CHAdeMO rapid-charge socket. Early versions of the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and the Kia Soul EV also relied on CHAdeMO for DC charging. These models make up a substantial share of the second-hand EV market, and their owners watch the rapid-charging network shrink every year as operators prioritise CCS investments.

This isn't a future worry, it's happening now. Major UK charge point operators, including Pod Point and Osprey, have publicly stated plans to reduce or eliminate CHAdeMO sockets in new installs. Existing CHAdeMO units at older sites are being retired and replaced with CCS-only or dual-socket hardware, with the latter becoming less common as operators weigh the cost of running two DC sockets against falling demand.

Day-to-day driving within a city works fine on home charging and Type 2 AC top-ups. Motorway journeys are a different story, forcing CHAdeMO drivers to plan routes obsessively around the dwindling supply of working CHAdeMO rapid chargers. This network erosion is already showing up in prices: CHAdeMO EVs depreciate faster than equivalent CCS models, reflecting charging stress and buyer hesitation about future usability.

Used EV Buyers in 2024: What You Need to Know About Connector Compatibility

Shopping for a used electric vehicle in the UK? Connector compatibility deserves a spot high on your list, alongside battery condition, service history, and warranty options. A CCS connector gives you the broadest access to the UK's current and future rapid-charging network. A car with only CHAdeMO for DC charging carries a tangible infrastructure risk that will likely get worse over the next three to five years as the network continues its shift to CCS.

Before buying, pin down exactly which connectors the vehicle has. Many used EV adverts describe charging capability vaguely or incorrectly. Check the owner's manual or the manufacturer's UK website for the actual specs. Confirm the car even has a DC rapid-charge inlet, some older entry-level EVs were sold without one, limiting them to AC charging only, which severely restricts long-distance driving regardless of which standard is at stake.

Think about the practical costs too. A CHAdeMO vehicle means longer stops at remaining CHAdeMO chargers, tedious route planning, and likely further depreciation. A well-maintained used EV with a CCS connector, even one with modest range, puts you within reach of a growing network of ultra-rapid chargers. Before you commit, also check the vehicle's dashboard warning lights to avoid picking up hidden faults, you can check what your warning light means to identify any potential issues.

FAQs and Bottom Line: Making Sense of EV Charger Standards

With three standards in play and an infrastructure landscape that keeps shifting, UK drivers ask specific, practical questions about how connector standards affect their ownership experience. The section below answers the most common ones, then offers a straightforward bottom line to guide your decisions about EV ownership, charging access, and used car purchases.

Here's the straightforward takeaway: Type 2 is your everyday AC connector, CCS is the future of UK rapid charging, and CHAdeMO is a legacy standard in decline. Knowing which applies to any EV you own or plan to buy isn't optional, it's fundamental to understanding the full ownership experience and whether the vehicle will stay usable on UK roads.

As the public charging network matures and ultra-rapid CCS hubs spread across motorway corridors and urban centres, the gap between CCS and CHAdeMO vehicles will only widen. Buyers who choose wisely today, prioritising CCS compatibility and confirming connector specifications before purchase, will find the EV ownership journey far smoother than those dealing with the infrastructure mismatches of an earlier era.

What is the difference between Type 2 and CCS connectors?

Type 2 is a seven-pin AC connector typically used for home and public slow-to-fast AC charging, delivering up to approximately 22 kW. CCS (Combined Charging System) typically adds two DC pins below Type 2 for rapid charging, generally enabling speeds ranging from approximately 50 kW to 350 kW. Most new UK EVs use a single CCS inlet that handles both AC and DC charging through the same socket.

Is CHAdeMO still supported at UK public charging stations?

CHAdeMO is still available at many existing UK rapid chargers, but new installations are overwhelmingly CCS-only. Major operators are phasing out CHAdeMO as equipment reaches end of life. While CHAdeMO coverage exists at older motorway and retail sites, its availability is declining steadily, making long-distance journey planning harder for CHAdeMO vehicle owners in the UK.

Can I use an adapter to charge a CHAdeMO car at a CCS charger?

No. There is no commercially available, widely supported adapter that allows a CHAdeMO vehicle to charge at a CCS rapid charger, or vice versa, for DC fast charging. The two systems use different communication protocols and connector designs. This incompatibility is a hardware limitation, not a software problem that software updates or aftermarket accessories can fix.

Do all new EVs sold in the UK use Type 2 and CCS connectors?

Almost universally, yes. Since 2022, every mainstream EV launched in the UK, from European, Korean, and American brands, uses Type 2 for AC and CCS for DC rapid charging. Tesla was the main holdout with its proprietary connector, but Tesla has since switched UK Superchargers and new cars to CCS compatibility, further cementing the standard across the UK.

What should I check about EV connectors before buying a used electric car?

Confirm the exact connector types: Type 2 for AC (standard on almost all EVs) and whether the car has a DC rapid-charge inlet, and if so, CCS or CHAdeMO. Verify this against manufacturer specifications rather than trusting the listing description alone. Prioritise CCS for long-term network access and check battery health and service history alongside connector compatibility.

Bottom Line

EV charger connector standards define how useful any electric vehicle is in the UK. Type 2 covers everyday AC charging. CCS is the present and future of rapid DC charging. CHAdeMO is a legacy standard in decline. Used car buyers especially must verify connector compatibility before purchase, a CCS-equipped EV offers far greater long-term network access than a CHAdeMO alternative at an equivalent price.
